subject: physics
title: Mass defect and binding energy
key_idea: A nucleus has less mass than its separate nucleons. The missing mass, the mass defect, is the energy that binds the nucleus together, given by E = mc². Binding energy per nucleon shows how stable a nucleus is.

blocks.text: Mass and energy are equivalent. Any change in the energy of a system comes with a change in its mass.

blocks.label: Mass–energy equivalence
where: ΔE = change in energy in J
Δm = change in mass in kg

items: E = mc² applies to all energy changes, but the mass change is only noticeable in nuclear reactions.
A reaction that releases energy loses mass. One that absorbs energy gains mass.
The mass of a nucleus is much smaller than the kilogram, so it is given in atomic mass units.

items.meaning: One twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom. 1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.
A unit of energy. 1 MeV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ J.

items: The two units link: **1 u = 931.5 MeV**.
To convert, multiply a mass in u by 931.5 to give the energy in MeV.
Mass in kg is found by multiplying the mass in u by 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷.
Energy released or absorbed in a reaction is ΔE = c²Δm.
A reaction that releases energy loses mass.

blocks.text: A nucleus weighs less than the protons and neutrons it contains. This section covers why, and how to calculate the energy involved.

items.meaning: The difference between the mass of the separate nucleons and the mass of the nucleus.
The energy needed to separate a nucleus into its individual nucleons. It is also the energy released when the nucleus forms.
The binding energy divided by the number of nucleons. It measures how stable a nucleus is.

items: Work must be done to pull a nucleus apart, so the separate nucleons have more energy and more mass.
The mass defect is the mass equivalent of the binding energy.
A higher binding energy per nucleon means a more stable nucleus.

items: Mass defect is the mass lost when nucleons bind to form a nucleus.
Binding energy = c²Δm, or Δm in u × 931.5 MeV.
Higher binding energy per nucleon means a more stable nucleus.

sections.heading: The binding energy per nucleon curve

blocks.text: Plotting binding energy per nucleon against nucleon number shows which reactions release energy.

diagram.alt: Binding energy per nucleon rises steeply for very light nuclei, peaks at iron-56 at about 8.8 MeV, then falls slowly for heavier nuclei.

items: The curve rises steeply to helium-4, which is unusually stable, then more slowly to a peak of about 8.8 MeV per nucleon at iron-56.
Beyond iron-56 it falls gently, to about 7.6 MeV per nucleon for uranium-238.
Joining light nuclei (**fusion**) gives a nucleus with a higher binding energy per nucleon, so energy is released.
Splitting a heavy nucleus (**fission**) gives fragments with a higher binding energy per nucleon, so energy is released.
Energy released = total binding energy after minus total binding energy before.

blocks.label: Energy released in a reaction
where: Δm = total mass before minus total mass after, in kg

items: If the total mass after the reaction is less than before, energy is released.
If it is greater, energy must be supplied, so the reaction absorbs energy.
Use nuclear masses, or atomic masses if the electrons balance on both sides.
Iron-56 has the highest binding energy per nucleon, so it is the most stable.
Fusion of light nuclei and fission of heavy nuclei both move towards the peak and release energy.
Energy released = c² × (mass before − mass after).

checks.a: The difference between the total mass of the separated nucleons and the mass of the nucleus they form.

checks.q: A reaction has a total mass loss of 3.0 × 10⁻²⁹ kg. Calculate the energy released.
Explain, using the binding energy per nucleon curve, why energy is released when a uranium nucleus splits.
checks.a: Uranium is a heavy nucleus with a lower binding energy per nucleon than the fragments formed. The fragments are nearer the peak, so the products are more tightly bound and the difference is released as energy.

items: You may be asked to mark on the curve the regions where fission or fusion releases energy.
The right-hand side of the peak is the region for fission. The left-hand side is the region for fusion.
Knowing the physics of nuclear energy lets society weigh up its benefits and risks when it makes decisions about energy.
